catalog_quote: 2.3. Stress. Stress patterning in Djambarrpuyŋu is largely predictable. ... In Yolŋu languages a number of investigators have used the term stress group to capture a somewhat different system of stress assignment. Each stress group consists of one to three syllables (see Wood 1978 and Waters 1980b). In this approach stress appears on the initial syllable of a stress group and the initial syllable of a word tends to carry primary stress. [p.63] The facts of stress patterning in Djambarrpuyŋu require an approach of this kind. In the following examples ' indicates primary stress and " secondary stress. /'Tja:l/ "want" /'PuKmaK/ "all" /'Puthuru/ "ear" /'Thama"rranTji/ "clan surname" /'nhuma"laŋKal/ "2/3pl-OBL" /'ŋurru"pandala/ "Bush Apple" /'Tjakada"yanPi/ "animal sp." /'Kuya"ŋanhawuy/ "thoughts" (plus FOURTH plus ASS) ... /'lithan"mara"nhamirr/ dry (plus CAUS+FOURTH+PROP) As with other Yol…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and all example words are verbatim on thesis pp. 62-63 (PDF pp. 86-87) of the Wilkinson 1991 scan we hold, read as page images. (2) Deciding source: Wilkinson 1991 is the language's only reference grammar (727 pp PhD, Glottolog 'grammar'; LINCOM 2012 reprint), so the primary-stress coding rests on the standard description, but its stress section is a one-page impressionistic statement borrowing the Yolŋu 'stress group' analysis from Wood 1978/Waters. A better stress source exists: Jepson 2019, a 363-pp Melbourne PhD devoted to Djambarrpuyŋu prosody, now downloaded (open, Minerva Access). sources.citation: Jepson, Kathleen. 2025. Contrastive vowel length and segment duration in production and perception in Djambarrpuyŋu. Laboratory Phonology 16(1): 1-49. doi:10.16995/labphon.10161 (open access).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'In Djambarrpuyŋu, the vowel length contrast is restricted to the first syllable of the word, a position which is also the putative location of fixed word stress (Wilkinson, 2012).' ... 'The restriction of contrastive vowel length to the initial syllable (i.e., the stressed syllable) is commonly reported for Pama-Nyungan languages'.
sources.note: Peer-reviewed OA statement that word stress is fixed initial and coincides with the only position licensing contrastive vowel length; supports the vowel-length remark in our locator.

sources.citation: Jepson, Kathleen Margaret. 2019. Prosody, prominence and segments in Djambarrpuyŋu. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne. hdl:11343/227802 (363 pp).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. iv: 'Word stress patterns previously reported for Djambarrpuyŋu include primary stress on the initial syllable and second stresses assigned to alternating odd syllables through a word or to the first syllable in suffixing morphemes. ... The results of a quantitative acoustic analysis partially support the previous description. The initial syllable of words does have the highest fundamental frequency of all syllables within a word. However, other correlates of prominence ... are not found in the data. Furthermore, evidence for secondary stress ... is not found'. p. 184: 'There was no support
sources.locator: Abstract p. iv; sec. 1.2.2.5 'Previous treatment of stress' pp. 14-15; ch. 5 'Results—Primary stress' pp. 163ff; sec. 5.8 'Chapter summary' p. 184
sources.note: Dedicated acoustic study of Djambarrpuyŋu word stress (ch. 5) that tests Wilkinson's impressionistic stress-group account; confirms initial primary stress, finds no acoustic secondary stress — should be cited alongside Wilkinson and the the secondary-stress rule annotated.
